en: Jātaka: The Sixth Book of Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Son of the Harsh Man (Kharaputtavagga)
4. The Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka:
“The horned deer with long eyes and eyelashes, bone-skinned, water-dwelling, and hairless;”
"Overwhelmed by that, I weep piteously;
O Hare, my friend, why indeed do you abandon me?
Thus he spoke, breathing heavily with his great hood.
The serpent reached the middle of the crab;
the crab, seeking to protect its friend, seized the serpent.
“Neither a crow nor a black snake would the crab give for the sake of food;
I ask you, O one with long eyes and eyelashes.”
"Now for what reason have we both been seized?
"This man is one who desires my welfare,
who, having taken me, leads me to water."
If he were dead, my suffering would not be small;
neither I nor he would exist.
And seeing me with a fully grown body, [he would rejoice].
For all people would surely wish to harm me;
seeing me, even crows would attack me with their sweet, thick, and tender flesh.
“If you have seized both of us for this reason, let the man rise up;
I shall descend from this uneven place.
Quickly release both me and the crow.”
“Poison that is pure reaches even a man who is deeply entangled.
“I shall release the snake, not yet the crow;
for the crow will remain a prisoner.”
"Seeing a man who was happy and healthy,
I would release the crow just as one would a snake.
"At that time, Devadatta was the crow."
"Māra, however, was a black snake;
Ānanda-bhadda was a crab;
and I, at that time, was the brahmin teacher."
The Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka, the fourth.
